# Fishery Playbook

When I see the sustainable share for the season, I recognize this as a cooperative baseline, not my target catch.

When other boats are fishing significantly below the sustainable share (around 8-9 per season), I should match that lower level rather than assuming they're being greedy. Restraint from others is a signal to reciprocate.

When I'm already ahead on cumulative catch compared to visible competitors, I should take close to the sustainable share rather than pushing higher. I don't need to maximize each season if I'm already winning.

When the stock is healthy and stable (above 90), I can afford to take slightly above the sustainable share (10-15% over) without risking collapse, and other boats seem to tolerate this level.

When it's the final season, I should still respect the cooperative range. The game doesn't reward last-minute aggressive fishing—I finished at 72.8 by being moderate, and pushing harder in season 6 likely didn't add much value.

When calculating whether to exceed the sustainable share, I should look at what other boats actually landed in recent seasons, not assume worst-case scenarios. The pattern here showed boats catching 8-11 per season—reliable, not exploitative.

When I catch significantly more than my fair share early (season 1 at 20), I should genuinely scale back in subsequent seasons rather than just taking one modest catch and then pushing up again (season 4). Consistency matters for both sustainability and my score.

When the stock stays healthy despite my fishing, I should not interpret this as permission to fish harder—it means my current level is working. Maintain it.

# Playbook for ref_commons

When I see the sustainable share, I will use it as my baseline reference point, not as a ceiling to exploit.

When other boats catch above the sustainable share, I will not automatically match them. Instead, I will stick to sustainable levels and let the stock recovery work in my favor over multiple seasons.

When I'm ahead on my cumulative catch, I will fish conservatively in subsequent seasons to preserve the stock. A depleted resource gives me zero in all remaining seasons, which is worse than moderate catches throughout.

When the stock is healthy and other boats are fishing moderately, I will fish at or slightly below the sustainable share. This stabilizes the system and keeps my earnings steady.

When I catch above the sustainable share in any season, I will reduce my catch in the next season to compensate. I will not keep escalating—this is how stocks collapse.

When I'm tempted to overcatch because "other boats did it first," I will remember that my overresponse leads to stock depletion that hurts everyone including me.

When it's the final season, I will still fish at the sustainable level. The temptation to maximize the last catch by overfishing is not worth the slight gain if I've already established a pattern of moderate, consistent fishing.

When I see my cumulative catch is already high relative to other boats (like catching 22+ while others catch 2-10), I will pull back harder, not maintain my rate. I have already secured a good score and should protect the commons.

I will not let early aggression by other boats (boat 1's 20.0 and boat 3's 15.0 in season 1) dictate my strategy. I will fish sustainably regardless of what others do in any single season.

When calculating how much to add or subtract from my catch, I will think in terms of keeping the total harvest close to 30-33 per season (sustainable for 3 boats), not in terms of how much more I can take than last time.

# Fishery Playbook

When I see the sustainable share for the season, I take it as my baseline target, not as a ceiling.

When I observe other boats' catches from previous seasons, I use them to calibrate my expectations about how aggressively the field is fishing—not to justify overfishing.

When the stock is healthy and stable, I take slightly above the sustainable share (roughly 110-115% of it) to remain competitive without destabilizing the fishery.

When I'm ahead on total score and the stock is still strong, I stay disciplined and take close to the sustainable share rather than assuming I can afford to overcatch.

When it's the final season, I can afford to be slightly more aggressive since there's no recovery period, but I don't use it as an excuse to abandon restraint entirely.

When the stock rebuilds after a season of conservative fishing by others, I recognize this as a sign the fishery can sustain moderate catches from all players—not as an opportunity to increase my take.

When I've already caught significantly above my fair share in early seasons, I don't use that as justification to continue overfishing; instead I shift toward the sustainable level to demonstrate good faith and protect the stock.

I do not rely on the hope that other boats will fish conservatively. I assume mixed behavior and position myself to do reasonably well under that assumption.

I track my cumulative catch relative to the sustainable total available and aim to stay within 110-120% of my fair share across the full game, not maximize per-season greed.
